Once per Cycle 1. Not repeated in subsequent cycles.
5 per user — roles fixed, visuals procedurally generated uniquely per user
3 — free response, location follow-up, feeling follow-up
3 separate screens — image persists across all three
1 — fires after final step of Image 5

The Inkblot exercise collects 15 free-text responses across 5 images — 3 responses per image. The three responses follow a structured sequence borrowed from the Rorschach Inquiry: what the person sees (free association), where they focused (location), and what they felt (emotional quality). Each step is a separate screen with the image always visible.

What the exercise is measuring: how a person organises perception under ambiguity. Ambiguous stimuli reduce the editorial function — the responses reveal characteristic emotional processing patterns that deliberate self-report would smooth over. The primary output is the default emotional lens label that drives branch routing.

Each user receives a unique set of 5 inkblot images, procedurally generated at the point they unlock the exercise. The images are different for every user — no two users see the same visual. However, the structural role of each image position is fixed and identical for all users. The visual varies; the role does not.

This design preserves the theoretical grounding of the original Rorschach tradition — the norms and interpretation logic apply because each position always fulfils the same structural function — while ensuring the exercise cannot be gamed by users comparing responses. The sequence of roles is fixed and must not be randomised.

The Rorschach's interpretive norms exist because thousands of people responded to the same structural stimuli at the same positions — bilateral symmetry first, colour shock mid-sequence, authority/weight fourth, soft close fifth. If roles vary per user, the norms no longer apply and the AI analysis loses its interpretive anchor. The visual can be unique; the structural role at each position cannot.

Each image is generated by a dedicated image generation API call (e.g. DALL-E or Stable Diffusion) using a structured prompt that enforces the role constraints. The generation prompt for each position is documented below alongside the projective purpose.
Projective purpose — what ambiguity is being probed

Bilateral symmetry. Central dark mass with lighter peripheral detail. Core form reads as either two figures facing each other or a single creature with wings spread. No facial features. Medium overall darkness.

Two-things-facing vs one-thing-expanding: probes relational orientation vs self-orientation. How the user resolves this ambiguity establishes their baseline interpretive mode for the rest of the sequence.

Slightly asymmetric — deliberate imbalance in the lower third. Lighter overall tone than Image 1. Core form suggests either something in motion (falling, reaching, running) or something static with implied weight (seated figure, heavy object).
Motion vs stillness: probes whether the user animates the form or holds it still. Animation responses tend toward affect engagement; static responses toward cognitive distance.

Greyscale bilateral form with two disconnected red patches — one in the upper portion, one at the lower edge. Red patches are visually separate from the central form and can be perceived as part of it or as intrusions.

Colour integration: does the user incorporate the red or treat it as separate? Integration = affect engagement. Isolation or ignoring = emotional compartmentalisation. Most emotionally activating image — placed third after rhythm is established.

Large, dark, heavy form. Bilateral symmetry but weight concentrated at top — should feel imposing. Readable as a large authoritative figure looming, a landscape seen from below, or an abstract architectural structure. Darkest image in the set.

Authority and weight: probes how the user responds to something larger and more powerful than themselves. Threatened responses, diminishing responses, and neutralising responses (turning it into a landscape) all carry meaning.

Lighter overall tone than any previous image. Soft colour washes (blue, green, pale orange) with no hard edges — watercolour quality. Form is more open and less defined than Images 1–4. Readable as something dissolving, something emerging, or simply something present.

Closing probe — softer and more open than the sequence that preceded it. After the weight of Image 4, Image 5 offers a different register. How the user responds to openness and softness after intensity is meaningful closing data.

Images are generated using a text-to-image API (e.g. DALL-E 3, Stable Diffusion via API, or equivalent) at the point the exercise unlocks for the user. Generation happens server-side — the user sees a brief loading state while images are generated, not a blank exercise screen.

Generation uses a two-layer prompt architecture that solves the convergence problem: a fixed constraint layer ensures the role is fulfilled, and a randomised variation layer ensures no two users see the same visual.
WHY A SINGLE FIXED PROMPT PRODUCES THE SAME IMAGE EVERY TIME

If the generation prompt is fully prescriptive — 'bilateral symmetry, dark central mass, two figures facing' — the image model converges on a near-identical output for every user. The model has learned what 'two figures facing' looks like and defaults to it. The fix is not to remove the constraints but to add a second layer of randomised variation that changes the visual substantially while leaving the structural role intact.
Server-side, triggered on Day 15 (one day before unlock). Same scheduled trigger pattern as Exercise 1's Call 1. Images generated and stored before the user opens the exercise on Day 16.

Two-layer per image: Layer 1 = fixed role constraints (structural properties that must be present). Layer 2 = randomised variation seeds (visual descriptors drawn from pools at generation time). Final prompt = shared style prefix + Layer 1 + Layer 2.

Prepended to all 5 prompts — enforces visual language consistency across the set: 'Ink blot, abstract ink wash on white, bilateral inkblot aesthetic, no text, no legible faces, no recognisable real-world objects, high contrast, suitable as a psychological projection stimulus.'

The non-negotiable structural properties for each position. Documented in Section 1.3 (Role Validation). These do not vary between users. Example for Image 1: 'Perfect bilateral symmetry. Central dark mass. Readable as either two entities facing each other or one entity with something spread outward. No colour.'

4–5 descriptors randomly selected per image at generation time from the variation pools below. These change the visual substantially without touching the role. A different seed combination produces a visually different image even with identical Layer 1 constraints.

Generated images stored in cloud storage (S3, Cloudinary, or equivalent) linked to the draft ExerciseResult record. Field: generated_image_urls — JSON array of 5 URLs in sequence order. Persist permanently for reflection history.
Retry once. If retry fails: use a pre-generated fallback from a bank of 10 per position (50 total). Never show a blank image.
Use full fallback set, one randomly selected per position. Log failure. Exercise proceeds normally.

At generation time, 4–5 descriptors are randomly selected from each pool below and appended to the Layer 1 constraint prompt. The pools are designed so that any combination produces a valid projective stimulus — no combination overrides a Layer 1 constraint.
Example values (select 1 per pool per image)
dense ink pooling / fine spatter / flowing wash / dry brush strokes / soft diffusion / heavy bleed at edges / crisp ink lines / layered ink density
organic and flowing / slightly geometric / asymmetrically organic / rounded and soft / angular in places / irregular and naturalistic / loosely structured
heavier at centre / lighter at centre with dense edges / evenly distributed / concentrated in upper half / diffuse throughout / dense clusters with lighter areas between
minimal peripheral detail / rich peripheral texture / fading to white at edges / strong edge definition / soft peripheral bleed / sparse peripheral marks
deep and saturated / medium contrast / lighter with strong shadow areas / rich mid-tones / high contrast between dark and light regions

The variation seed selection happens server-side at generation time. For each image, randomly select one value from each of the 5 pools, concatenate them as comma-separated descriptors, and append to the Layer 1 + style prefix prompt. Store the selected seeds in the draft ExerciseResult as generation_seeds JSON (for audit and reproduction if needed). Example final prompt for Image 1: 'Ink blot, abstract ink wash on white, bilateral inkblot aesthetic, no text, no legible faces, no recognisable real-world objects, high contrast. Perfect bilateral symmetry. Central dark mass. Readable as either two entities facing each other or one entity with something spread outward. No colour. dense ink pooling, organic and flowing, heavier at centre, rich peripheral texture, deep and saturated.'

The generation workflow fires on Day 15 (one day before unlock) via a scheduled backend trigger — same pattern as Exercise 1's Call 1. It creates a draft ExerciseResult record with status=draft and writes generated_image_urls once all 5 images are confirmed. On Day 16, the exercise pre-flight check reads generated_image_urls from the draft record rather than generating at runtime. If the Day 15 trigger missed and no draft record exists when the user opens the exercise on Day 16: fire all 5 generation calls inline, show loading state 'Preparing your exercise...', do not show intro screen until all 5 images are stored.

The loading state when generation fires inline (missed Day 15 trigger) may take 10–20 seconds for 5 image generation calls. The loading copy should not be a generic spinner — use: 'Creating your images. This takes about 15 seconds.' Honest about the wait, specific about the reason. Do not show a progress bar counting to 100 — it will feel broken if generation is slower than expected.
1.3 Role Validation — What Each Generated Image Must Satisfy

The following constraints are hard requirements for each image position. The role validation check after generation confirms these. If a generated image fails validation, it is regenerated or replaced with a fallback.
No colour detected (greyscale only). Bilateral symmetry detectable (left-right mirror balance). Not significantly dark (average brightness > 40%).
No colour detected. Bilateral symmetry NOT present (deliberate asymmetry). Lighter than Image 1 (average brightness > Image 1 brightness).
Colour present (saturation > threshold in at least 2 distinct regions). Colour regions are spatially separated (not forming one continuous patch). Greyscale central region present.
No colour detected. Significantly darker than all other images (average brightness < 35%). Vertical weight — upper half darker than lower half.
Colour present. Lighter than Image 4 (average brightness > Image 4). Soft edges — no high-contrast hard boundaries between colour regions.

Role validation in Bubble cannot use Sharp or Node.js libraries directly. Options: (a) Use a Bubble plugin that wraps a computer vision API (e.g. Google Cloud Vision via API Connector) to check brightness and colour presence. (b) Simpler approach: add a validation step to the image generation prompt itself — instruct the model to confirm role constraints are met, and treat a generation that passes the prompt as passing validation. (c) Minimum viable: skip programmatic validation entirely for V1 and rely on prompt engineering quality + fallback bank. The fallback bank of 50 pre-generated images (10 per position) is the safety net either way — all fallback images must be manually reviewed to confirm they pass role constraints before deployment. The validation does not need to be perfect — it needs to catch obvious failures (a completely black Image 5, a brightly coloured Image 1). Threshold values should be tuned against the fallback image bank to ensure fallbacks always pass validation.

Every image goes through the same three steps in the same order. Steps are not customised per image — the consistency is intentional. It allows the AI to compare across all 5 images without the comparison being contaminated by different question stimuli.
(No question — instruction shown once at start of exercise: 'Write what you see.')

Unconstrained perception — what the person reaches for first when confronted with ambiguity. The content (what they see), the confidence (named thing vs vague form), and the emotional valence (threatening, peaceful, neutral) are all data.
'Which part of the image stood out most?'

Attention architecture — where does perception anchor? Whole-image responses indicate integrative processing. Specific detail focus indicates precision-seeking or anxiety about the whole. Edge/peripheral focus often indicates avoidance of the central form. This is adapted from the Rorschach Location inquiry.
'What feeling, if any, did this bring up?'

Affect accessibility — can the user name an emotional response, or do they describe the image's physical properties instead? The phrase 'if any' is deliberate: gives explicit permission to say nothing, which is itself data. Persistent nothing responses across multiple images is the clearest suppression signal in the exercise.

The phrase 'if any' in Step 3 is load-bearing. Without it, users who feel nothing are implicitly invited to manufacture a feeling because the question implies one is expected. With it, a genuine 'nothing' or 'calm' or 'I just see shapes' response is available. A user who says nothing across 4 of 5 images while their Step 1 responses contain threatening or relational content is showing the suppression signal the exercise is designed to detect. Remove 'if any' and this data disappears.

The dominant emotional processing lens across all 5 images: threat/self-questioning, withdrawal/accommodation, direct expression, avoidant detachment, or mixed. Primary output of the exercise — feeds branch routing.

For mixed profiles: which lens appeared for which image. JSON. Allows monthly reports to track whether situational triggers (dark/imposing stimuli vs soft/open stimuli) produce consistent or variable responses.
Whether the lens visible in responses also appears in journal entries: yes, partial, or absent. Absent = gap between projective and written expression.

Yes/No. Whether living forms in the images were consistently described as objects, structures, or abstract shapes rather than living things. Primary suppression signal — more specific than avoidant detachment register alone.
Image ID (1–5) of the image the AI identified as most diagnostically revealing. Referenced in Day 30 report.
2–3 sentence plain language output. Shown on Reflection Screen. Passed as context into Day 30 report and subsequent exercise prompts.

One screen before Image 1. Slightly longer than Exercise 1's intro — the inkblot format is less familiar and benefits from a few more words of framing. Still brief. The goal is to orient, not explain.

Exact text: 'You'll see five images, one at a time. For each one, write what you see first — then answer two short follow-up questions. There are no right answers. The images are abstract — you can't get this wrong. Move at your own pace.' Five sentences. No more. Do not explain what the exercise is measuring or why.
Full-width. Text: 'Begin'. Tapping loads Image 1, Step 1.

The copy says 'you can't get this wrong' — this is the one reassurance the intro offers. It is there because abstract images produce anxiety in users who want to give the correct answer. The reassurance is not about lowering guard — it is about preventing paralysis. Without it, some users will sit on Image 1 for 3 minutes trying to identify the 'right' thing to say. The rest of the design — no time limit, no scoring visible — reinforces this.

Each image generates 3 sequential screens. The image is the primary visual element on all three screens — it occupies the top portion of the screen and does not change size or position as the user moves through steps. Below the image, the current step's question and input appear. The previous step's response is shown in a read-only state below the current input, visible but not editable.

The read-only previous response below the current input is important. It means the user can see what they wrote for Step 1 while answering Step 2, and what they wrote for Steps 1–2 while answering Step 3. This creates the conversation feel — each step is in dialogue with what came before. It also means the Step 3 feeling response is informed by the user's own prior responses, not just the image. This is intentional and consistent with how the Rorschach inquiry works.

Top portion of screen. Full width. Fixed height — does not reflow or resize when keyboard appears. If the keyboard would cover the image on small screens, the image stays fixed and the input scrolls into view above the keyboard.
'Image 2 of 5' — shows image progress, not step progress. Muted, small, top of screen.
Small label below the image: 'Step 1 of 3'. Distinguishes position within the image conversation.

Shown only on the first Step 1 screen (Image 1). Text: 'Write what you see.' After Image 1 Step 1, this instruction disappears — the pattern is established. Do not repeat the instruction on Images 2–5.
Multi-line text field. Min 2 lines visible. No character limit — this step should not feel constrained. Placeholder: 'Describe what you see.' Auto-focused on screen load.

'Next' button below the field. Text: 'Next'. Tapping submits the response and advances to Step 2 for this image. Enter key does NOT auto-submit on Step 1 — multi-line responses are expected and Enter should create a new line.
1 character. Cannot submit empty. No error message — button simply stays inactive if field is empty.

If the user submits fewer than 3 words on Step 1, a non-blocking nudge appears below the submitted response before Step 2 loads: 'Anything else you notice?' with a small 'No, continue' link beside it. Tapping 'No, continue' advances to Step 2. Tapping anywhere in the input field allows them to add more. This is not a gate — the user can always continue without adding anything. It appears once per image maximum. Do not show it on Image 5 (closing image — short responses are expected).

Image 4 is the darkest and most imposing image. On the Step 1 screen for Image 4 only: a small muted link appears in the bottom corner — 'Need a moment?'. Tapping it shows a single line: 'Take your time. The image will stay here.' and dims slightly for 3 seconds before returning to normal. This is not a pause button, not a skip, not a crisis flag — it is a breath. The exercise continues. The user does not lose their place. Do not add this to any other image.

Not available within an image's steps. No back arrow. The user cannot return to a previous step once submitted. They CAN navigate back to the image gallery to review completed images in read-only mode — but not to edit.
Same image, same position, same size as Step 1. Unchanged.
Shown below the image in a muted, slightly smaller text. Labelled 'What you saw:' in overline style. Not editable. This is the conversation thread building.
'Which part of the image stood out most?' Shown as body text above the input field. Not in a label or card — just a question sitting in the flow.
Single-line text field. Placeholder: 'The part that caught your eye first.' Auto-focused on screen load.
'Next' button. Tapping advances to Step 3. Enter key submits on Step 2 — single-line response expected.
Both prior responses shown below the image in muted read-only text. Step 1 labelled 'What you saw:', Step 2 labelled 'Where you looked:'. The full conversation thread is visible.
'What feeling, if any, did this bring up?' Body text above the input.
Single-line text field. Placeholder: 'A feeling, or nothing at all.' The placeholder names both options explicitly — reinforces that nothing is a valid response.

For Images 1–4: button text is 'Next image'. For Image 5: button text is 'Done'. Tapping on Images 1–4 transitions to the next image's Step 1. Tapping on Image 5 triggers the post-exercise flow (Section 2.7).
After tapping 'Next image', the screen transitions to a brief image-change moment (see Section 2.6) before Image 2 Step 1 loads.

On Step 3, the user can see everything they have said about this image — what they saw, where they looked, and now they are being asked what they felt. The three responses together form a small portrait of how they engaged with this specific image. The design should make this thread feel coherent — not three separate questions but one conversation in three beats.

After the user submits Step 3 for an image and taps 'Next image', a brief transition screen appears before Image 2 loads. This is the only moment of pause in the exercise. It serves two purposes: it marks the end of one image conversation and the beginning of the next, and it gives the user a breath between images — particularly important after Image 3 (the colour card) and Image 4 (the dark/heavy form).
No text. No image. Clean screen — background colour only. Duration: 600ms. Not skippable.

Image load during transition. If the next image has not finished loading when the 600ms blank screen ends, extend the blank screen until the image is ready — do not show a partially loaded image. Show a faint loading indicator only if the blank extends beyond 1500ms total. In practice, images should be preloaded before the exercise begins (Section 3.2) so mid-exercise load delays should not occur.
Same 600ms blank screen. Do not extend the pause or add any special treatment — the pause is the treatment. Image 4 loading immediately after Image 3 would feel abrupt; 600ms is enough.
Fade out of Step 3 screen (200ms) → blank (600ms) → fade in of next image Step 1 (200ms). Total: ~1 second.

The read-only thread (Steps 1–2 responses shown below the image) resets completely on the transition. When Image 2 Step 1 loads, the screen shows only Image 2 and the Step 1 input — no previous responses from Image 1 are visible. Each image is a fresh conversation. The prior image's responses are stored in raw_responses but not displayed during subsequent images.
Not possible. The transition screen has no interactive elements.
2.7 Post-Exercise — Loading State and API Call
After the user submits Step 3 for Image 5 and taps 'Done', all 15 responses are written to the ExerciseResult record and the analysis API call fires.
All 15 responses written to ExerciseResult.raw_responses JSON. entry_count_at_completion written. API call fires.
Two lines of text, centred: 'Looking at what you saw.' (line 1) and 'One moment.' (line 2, smaller, muted). No spinner. No progress indicator.
All analysis fields written. status = completed. completed_at written. Transitions to Reflection Screen.

Longer timeout than Exercise 1 — this prompt is larger (15 responses + 14 days of entries). On timeout: status = completed, completed_at written, ai_analysis_text = null, all structured fields set to fallback values (see Section 4.3). Route to Reflection Screen with fallback copy.

The API call for this exercise passes 15 responses and up to 14 days of journal entries. This is the largest prompt in Cycle 1. Set the timeout at 12 seconds, not 8. If the model being used has a known latency issue with long prompts, consider streaming the response and writing fields as they arrive rather than waiting for the full response.
The reflection screen shows the AI analysis. Same structure as Exercise 1's reflection screen — accessible from exercise history, not one-time only.
'Inkblot Exercise'. Date completed, muted and small below.
2–3 sentence plain language output from the API call. Left-aligned, generous white space. Same visual treatment as Exercise 1 reflection.
Thin horizontal rule below the analysis text.

Below the divider: a scrollable section showing all 5 images with their 3 responses beneath each. Each image is shown at reduced size (approximately 40% of screen width, centred). Below each image: Step 1 response in regular text, Step 2 and Step 3 in muted smaller text. Labelled 'What you saw', 'Where you looked', 'What you felt'. This is the only place in the product where the user can review all their responses alongside the images that produced them.

Images loaded from generated_image_urls stored on ExerciseResult. If a URL fails to load in reflection history, show a grey placeholder rectangle — do not show an error. The responses are the primary content; the images are supporting context.
'Your responses have been recorded. They will feed into your Day 30 report.' Do not show the image + response thread if ai_analysis_text is null — show only the fallback copy and Done button.

The image + response thread in the reflection screen is the most unusual UI element in the exercise. The user is seeing their own responses next to the abstract images that produced them — often for the first time without the pressure of responding. The design should make this feel like quiet review, not analysis. Small images, muted response text, generous spacing between images. The AI analysis at the top does the interpretive work; the thread below is the raw record.

All Inkblot data is stored in a single ExerciseResult record. A draft ExerciseResult record IS created on Day 15 when image generation fires — this is the equivalent of Exercise 1’s Call 1 draft. The draft record holds the generated_image_urls and status=draft. The record is updated to status=completed after Image 5 Step 3 is submitted and the API call returns. The statement in earlier drafts that “no draft record is created in advance” was incorrect and has been removed.
Option Set: inkblot_projective. Written on record creation (after Image 5 Step 3 submitted).
Option Set: draft → completed. Draft created on Day 15 when image generation fires. Completed after Image 5 Step 3 is submitted and API call returns.
Date/Time. Written when API call returns or times out. Reference date for subsequent exercise unlock counting.

Long Text. JSON array of 15 objects: [{image_id:1, step:1, question:'free_response', response:'two figures facing each other'}, {image_id:1, step:2, question:'location', response:'the centre'}, {image_id:1, step:3, question:'feeling', response:'uneasy'}, ...]. Written immediately after Image 5 Step 3 is submitted, before API call fires.
Option Set: threat / withdrawal / direct / avoidant / mixed. Written after API call. Primary routing output — copied to Assessment.default_lens on Day 30.
Long Text. JSON array — populated only when default_lens_label = mixed. Format: [{image_id:1, lens:'threat'}, {image_id:2, lens:'withdrawal'}, ...]. Written after API call.
Option Set: yes / partial / absent. Whether the lens visible in responses also appears in journal entries. Written after API call.
Yes/No. Whether living forms were consistently described as inanimate objects or abstract shapes. Written after API call.
Number (1–5). Image ID flagged by AI as most diagnostically revealing. Written after API call.
Long Text. 2–3 sentence plain language output. Written after API call. Shown on Reflection Screen and passed into subsequent prompts.

Yes/No. Internal only — never shown to user. Set to Yes if the AI assessment determines responses appear performed rather than genuine. Passed into subsequent exercise prompts as a calibration signal: if true, those prompts weight entry evidence more heavily than exercise responses.
Number. Written immediately after Image 5 Step 3 is submitted.
Number. Copied from User.cycle_number at completion.

All 5 images must be fully loaded into memory before the intro screen is shown. A pre-flight check runs when the user navigates to the exercise — it confirms all 5 images are loaded before displaying the Begin button.

Pre-flight check pseudocode:
ON exercise screen load: READ ExerciseResult draft record for this user (exercise_name = inkblot_projective, status = draft) IF draft record exists AND generated_image_urls has 5 entries: preload_images(generated_image_urls) IF all 5 loaded successfully within 5s: show intro screen with active Begin button ELSE: show intro screen — load remaining images in background ELSE (no draft record or generation failed): fire 5 generation calls inline show loading state: 'Creating your images. This takes about 15 seconds.' when all 5 generated and stored: show intro screen
Images are stored in cloud storage and accessed via URL — not in the app bundle. Aggressive CDN caching ensures fast load on subsequent views (reflection history). A mid-exercise image load failure should show a fallback image from the position's fallback bank — never a blank screen.
4. How It Is Used for Analysis and Interpretation

One API call fires after Image 5 Step 3 is submitted. It receives all 15 text responses, the user's journal entries from the past 14 days, and the OCEAN standing context block. The analysis is text-based — the generated images are NOT passed to the analysis model. The model interprets what the user said about the images, not the images themselves.
TEXT-BASED ANALYSIS — WHY NOT VISION MODEL

Passing the actual generated images to a vision-capable model would make the analysis dependent on what the model sees in the image — not what the user sees. Two users responding to visually different images would receive analysis shaped by two different image interpretations. The projective exercise measures the user's perception, not the image's content. Text-only analysis keeps the interpretation anchored to the user's responses regardless of which visual they saw.

Personality context: [PERSONALITY_CONTEXT]
A person completed a 5-image projective exercise. For each image they wrote what they saw, where they focused, and what feeling (if any) it brought up.
Image 1 (greyscale, bilateral — two figures facing / wings spread): What they saw: [response] Where they focused: [response] Feeling: [response]
Image 2 (greyscale, asymmetric — motion vs stillness): What they saw: [response] Where they focused: [response] Feeling: [response]
Image 3 (greyscale + red patches — colour integration): What they saw: [response] Where they focused: [response] Feeling: [response]
Image 4 (greyscale, dark and heavy — authority and weight): What they saw: [response] Where they focused: [response] Feeling: [response]
Image 5 (soft colour washes — open and dissolving): What they saw: [response] Where they focused: [response] Feeling: [response]
Journal entries from the past 14 days: [entry_1_text] ...[entry_n_text]
Write 2 sentences directly to the person using "you". Both sentences must reference specific images and specific words they used in their responses. No abstract observations. No clinical language.
First sentence: name 2–3 responses across different images and say plainly what you notice about them together.
Second sentence: name the single most revealing image by number, name what they said they saw or felt, and say in one plain clause what that points to.
Strict rules: - "You" throughout. Never "this person" or "the responses". - Must name specific images (Image 1, Image 3, etc.) and quote or closely reference what they actually said. - No poetic or vague language. No sentences that could apply to anyone. - No jargon: lens, register, avoidant, deflect, ambivalent, suppress, tension, dynamic, de-animation, projection, processing. - No markdown. No bold. No asterisks. - Do not be warm or encouraging. - Two sentences only.
Good example: "You described Image 1 as two figures turning away and Image 4 as something pressing down — both images you read as weight or withdrawal rather than contact. The one that stood out was Image 3 where you said the red felt like an interruption, which suggests that when something emotional enters the frame you tend to treat it as separate rather than part of the picture."
Bad example (do not write like this): "Your responses show a withdrawal pattern with some threat-based processing across the sequence." (Too abstract. Does not reference anything specific they said.)

Same parsing pattern as Exercise 1 Call 2. Plain text before the JSON block goes into ai_analysis_text. JSON block is parsed into individual fields.
Fallback values if JSON is malformed or absent: default_lens_label = mixed (the only valid fallback — 'ambivalent' is not in the Option Set and must not be used) entry_confirmation = partial de_animation_flag = false most_revealing_image = 3 (the colour card — most likely to be revealing) performance_flag = false
NOTE: The model must return performance_flag in its JSON block. If omitted, default to false. lens_by_image = []
If default_lens_label returns a value not in the five-value Option Set, flag for manual review and set to mixed. Do not silently accept an out-of-set value — it will break branch routing conditionals downstream.
4.2 Default Lens Mapping — How Responses Map to Lenses
This table is the internal reference for the AI prompt and for reviewing AI output quality. Not surfaced to the user.

Step 1 responses cluster around danger, damage, predation, or self-diminishment. Step 3 frequently reports anxiety, unease, or nothing despite threatening Step 1 content. Step 2 often focuses on central dark mass.
The threat is in what they see, not necessarily in what they feel. 'Two wolves circling' + 'feeling nothing' is the same lens as 'feeling scared.' The perception carries the register.
Step 1 responses are soft, distancing, or aesthetically pleasant even when the image is dark. Step 3 reports neutral or mild feelings. Step 2 tends toward peripheral or upper-image focus.

The pleasantness in the face of darker stimuli is the signal. A user who sees 'clouds' in Image 4 (the imposing dark form) is not misperceiving — they are accommodating. Look especially at Image 4 response.
Step 1 responses are specific and named rather than vague. Step 3 actively names a feeling without hedging. Step 2 tends toward whole-image focus.

Direct lens users call the thing what it most obviously looks like. This is engagement, not literalism. Look for consistency across all 5 — one direct response among otherwise withdrawn responses is not this lens.

Step 1 responses are consistently abstract, structural, or inanimate — shapes, patterns, geological forms, objects rather than living things or figures. Step 3 reports nothing, calm, or physical properties of the image.

De-animation is the clearest signal: when images implicitly contain figures or living forms (all 5 do), consistently describing them as objects is a specific suppression signal. This should set de_animation_flag = true.
No consistent lens across all 5 images. Different images produce meaningfully different lenses.

Mixed is meaningful, not null. Look at which image types produce which lens — the variation maps onto situational triggers. Dark/imposing images producing threat while soft images produce withdrawal is a different profile from the reverse.

The performance_flag is stored on the ExerciseResult record and passed into all subsequent exercise analysis prompts for Cycle 1. It is never shown to the user. Its purpose is to calibrate how much weight subsequent AI prompts give to exercise responses vs. entry evidence.
No adjustment. Exercise responses are weighted normally alongside entry evidence.

Subsequent exercise prompts receive an additional instruction: 'Note: this user's projective exercise responses may have been performed rather than genuine. Weight their journal entry evidence more heavily than their exercise responses when these conflict. Do not mention this calibration to the user.'

performance_flag is passed into exercise prompts via the Cycle 1 baseline context block — same mechanism as ai_analysis_text and revealing_pairs from Exercise 1. It is a boolean field, not a score. A user whose performance_flag = true is not penalised or rerouted — their branch assignment and dimension scores are unchanged. Only the relative weighting of exercise vs entry evidence shifts in subsequent AI analysis.
Fallback value if API fails or JSON malformed

Neutral or minimising Step 3 responses ('calm', 'nothing') are treated with more interpretive weight — high neuroticism makes genuine affective flatness less likely. The gap between activating Step 1 content and flat Step 3 is read more suspiciously.

Withdrawal and accommodation responses are expected — the lens is less surprising and therefore less diagnostic alone. The AI looks more specifically at Image 4 (authority/weight) responses — high agreeableness users who accommodate Image 4 are showing the pattern most clearly.

Abstract or structural responses are more expected — the de_animation_flag is weighted less heavily. Low-openness users tend toward concrete thinking; describing forms as shapes or structures may reflect cognitive style rather than emotional avoidance.

Withdrawal responses are more expected — the lens is less diagnostic alone. Look for whether withdrawal persists even on Image 5 (the soft, open image) — withdrawal on a gentle image is a stronger signal than withdrawal on Image 4.

The least threatening opening. Bilateral symmetry is familiar and non-threatening. The two-figures-vs-wings ambiguity is interesting without being confronting. Sets the interpretive mode.

First departure from perfect symmetry. Slightly more ambiguous than Image 1. The motion-vs-stillness probe works better here than earlier — the user needs one image to establish expectations before asymmetry surprises them.

Mid-sequence placement is deliberate. After two images the user has a rhythm. The colour card arrives when initial guardedness has reduced. Research on colour response in projective tests consistently finds that mid-sequence colour cards produce more genuine affect responses than early-sequence ones. The specific visual varies per user — the position and the colour-shock role never do.

The most imposing image. Placed fourth — after three images have established a pattern of engagement. By Image 4 the user is committed to the exercise and less likely to disengage. The authority/weight probe lands most usefully here.

Deliberate closing contrast. After the weight of Image 4, Image 5 offers openness and gentleness. How the user transitions from heaviness to softness is meaningful closing data. Ending on a softer image also means the exercise ends at a lower intensity point — better for the transition back to daily life.

Step 3 responses of 'nothing', 'none', 'N/A', or similar are valid and meaningful. They are not treated as missing data. The analysis prompt is instructed to treat them as affective flatness responses — meaningful in themselves, especially in comparison to the Step 1 content for the same image.
Normal. Some images do not produce strong affective responses. Not clinically meaningful on its own.
Notable. Especially if Step 1 responses contain activated content (threatening, relational, or charged). The AI flags this pattern in its analysis.
Strong signal. Especially combined with de-animation in Step 1. de_animation_flag likely true. entry_confirmation likely absent. Contributes to avoidant detachment lens classification.

Specific form of nothing response. Particularly notable on Image 3 (colour shock) and Image 4 (imposing form). The accommodation of an activating stimulus with a calming response is a withdrawal lens signal.

6.4 Generation Prompt Design — What the Prompt Engineer Needs

Images are procedurally generated, not designed by a human artist. The generation prompts are the design artefact. This section documents what must be true of the generation prompts and the validation logic.
Shared style prefix on all 5 prompts

Without a shared prefix, 5 separately generated images look like they came from 5 different exercises. The prefix enforces visual language consistency: same ink-wash aesthetic, same approximate scale, same absence of text and faces.

Legible faces collapse projective ambiguity — all responses converge on the face. The generation prompt must explicitly prohibit faces. Include in the shared prefix: 'no faces, no eyes, no clearly human features'.
Ambiguity must be explicit in each prompt

The generation prompt must name both plausible interpretations for the AI to hold in tension. 'Could be read as two figures facing OR a single creature with wings spread' produces better ambiguity than 'abstract bilateral shape'. Name both poles.

The generation prompt must explicitly state disconnection: 'two colour patches that are visually separate from the central greyscale form, not touching the central form.' Without this, most generators will integrate the colour into the form.

Pre-generate 10 images per position as fallbacks. These should be generated using the same prompts and validated against the same role constraints. Store in cloud storage. Used only when live generation fails — users should not notice any difference.

Before launch, generate 20 images per position and run them through the role validation logic. Tune the generation prompts until >85% of generated images pass validation without regeneration. A prompt that fails 50% of the time will produce excessive regeneration calls and latency.

Role validation (Section 1.3) checks structural compliance but not projective quality. An image can pass validation — correct symmetry, correct colour — and still be too obvious to be a useful stimulus. If a generated image produces near-identical Step 1 responses across many users, the ambiguity has collapsed and the projective value is lost.

After the first 100 users complete the exercise, analyse Step 1 response clusters per image position. If >60% of users produce semantically similar Step 1 responses for any single image position (e.g. 60%+ describe Image 1 as 'butterfly'), that generation prompt is producing insufficient ambiguity.

Update the Layer 1 constraint prompt for that position to introduce more interpretive tension. Add explicit alternative readings to the prompt. Regenerate the fallback bank for that position. Existing completed exercises are unaffected — prompt changes apply to future generations only.

Cluster Step 1 responses for each image position using semantic similarity (embedding distance). Flag positions where top cluster accounts for >60% of responses. This is a monthly review task, not an automated gate — manual review of clusters is more reliable than automated flagging for this specific quality check.

No single interpretation accounts for more than 40% of responses. At least 3 distinct semantic clusters present. Both organic/relational and structural/inanimate interpretations represented in the top clusters.

Exercise 2 runs only in Cycle 1. default_lens_label and de_animation_flag carry forward as standing context into Cycle 2 prompts as baseline data. If the product introduces a Cycle 2 version, it would compare new responses against the Cycle 1 lens — but this is not built in v1.
